prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, bringing atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level of accuracy

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a discovery in the sense I try to apply first: a concrete result sitting at the centre of physics, from which the people can then be identified. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal let many atoms be trapped without shifting the clock transition, and Ye's group took the strontium lattice clock to coherence and systematic control at the 1e-18 level. The consequences are already realised and independently reproduced: international clock comparisons, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches, and the formal discussion of redefining the second. The credit is also unusually clean, two names for one idea and its decisive realisation, and every member ranked it, with six placing it in their top three. Broad support is not merit in itself, but here the scientific, attribution and maturity arguments all point the same way.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to the 2005 prize on frequency combs and the 2012 prize on control of individual quantum systems, which includes ion clocks. A committee could read lattice clocks as an incremental, if spectacular, continuation of optical frequency metrology. Second, other groups (Lemonde, Oates, Ludlow and others) made early contributions that fall outside the two credited names, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so some of the societal payoff is still prospective. I do not think these defeat the case, but they are real.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because a theory-predicted flat band met an experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in a clean, tunable platform that opened moire materials as a field.
responses.response: I agree this is a genuine discovery with a good prediction and experiment pairing, and I kept it in my top three. My difference is about maturity and attribution. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still contested, the field is moving fast, and Andrei's earlier STM evidence leaves a three-name split open to challenge, as you acknowledge yourself. The lattice clock has a stable interpretation and a settled credit, so I do not think it should wait for twistronics to settle. If the committee prefers the moire case, I would want the citation to rest on the flat-band prediction and the 2018 observations, not on the superconducting mechanism.

responses.point: Pearce puts topological insulators first as a conceptually deep, broadly influential and arguably overdue field, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the core trio.
responses.response: I share the view that topological insulators are overdue and ranked them second. The scientific case is stronger than for almost any other candidate. My hesitation is attribution under a three-person cap. Mele is essential to the Kane-Mele theory, Molenkamp to the HgTe experiment, and Hasan's three-dimensional ARPES work, along with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, falls outside any trio. I proposed Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, you proposed Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and that disagreement shows the credit is contestable in a way the clock credit is not. I would support this prize if the committee can agree on the scope, and it is my first alternative after B013 only because of that unresolved scope question.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture underlying essentially all superconducting quantum processors, with Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf covering theory and the two decisive experiments.
responses.response: The importance of circuit QED is clear, but I ranked it outside my preferred set because the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is so close in subject that the committee would be accused of returning to the same area immediately. Girvin, Huang and Majer are also missing from the three names. I would value hearing how you weigh that overlap, since your own ranking puts the clock second and may be the natural common ground.

responses.point: Kroll supports optical lattice clocks as measurement science that defines what we can know, and notes that overlap with earlier optical frequency prizes and the pending redefinition of the second are the main counterarguments.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and with the identification of the 2005 and 2012 overlap as the main risk. I would answer that Hall and Hansch were recognised for the frequency comb that makes optical clocks countable, and Wineland for single-ion control, whereas the lattice clock's distinct idea is many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength, which brought statistical gain and a different class of systematics. The pending redefinition of the second is a reason to act, not to wait, because the discovery's merit does not depend on the SI decision.

uncertainties: How the committee weighs overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes in optical frequency metrology.
Whether early contributions of other lattice-clock groups outside Katori and Ye require recognition or a modified citation.
If the committee turns to topological insulators or moire materials, how the three-person limit should be allocated (Mele, Hasan and Andrei remain unresolved).
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, Uppsala theory group) are in string theory and cosmology and none of them relates to any shortlisted candidate.
